beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear, with a short film for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Computational Skepticism for AI. You might think skepticism is just doubting everything. That's a mood. Here, skepticism is a method: a set of moves you run on a claim.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. Radical doubt: asking what would make a claim wrong. Induction: trusting a pattern because it held in the past. And falsifiable: a claim that names the result that would prove it wrong.

beats.narration_text: Not the eye roll. Not the person who is against everything. A method: a few moves you perform on a claim. They can be taught, and you can see whether someone did them. Three philosophers each donate one move.

beats.narration_text: The hard part isn't doubting what looks suspicious. It's doubting what looks right: fluent, specific, neatly formatted. That's when the moves matter most, and when the urge to skip them is strongest. The enemy isn't laziness. It's confidence.

beats.narration_text: Move one is from Day-cart. Take the claim and ask: what would have to be true for this to be wrong? The answers aren't a feeling. They're a checklist: the training data, the inputs, the setting it runs in. Each one, you can check.

beats.narration_text: In twenty twelve, the trading firm Knight Capital put new code on eight servers. A technician missed one, and no one noticed. On that eighth server, old code, unused since two thousand three, woke up. In about forty five minutes it made over four million trades, and Knight lost more than four hundred sixty million dollars, per the SEC. Ask what would make done wrong, and you check all eight.

beats.narration_text: Move two is from Hume. A model that was right a thousand times has no guarantee about the next time. Picture a turkey, fed every morning for a thousand days. Each meal makes it surer of the next. On day one thousand and one, the farmer comes with an axe.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft turkey beside a feeding tray; a day counter climbs 'day 1' to 'day 1,000' while an ink confidence curve rises ('confidence'); on 'day 1,001' the grain is gone and the curve drops straight down to a terracotta dot.

beats.narration_text: Big systems do it too. Google Flu Trends estimated flu from web searches. From August twenty eleven, it ran too high in one hundred of one hundred and eight weeks, per a paper in Science. A turkey with a spreadsheet. Its confidence belonged to the model, not to the world.

beats.narration_text: Move three is from Popper. A claim that can't be wrong isn't a claim yet. And piling up successes never proves one. No count of white swans proves that all swans are white. One black swan disproves it.

beats.narration_text: So hunt for the black swan. A sepsis alert model was running in hundreds of U.S. hospitals without an adequate outside test. When outside researchers ran one, on twenty seven thousand six hundred ninety seven patients, it missed about two of every three sepsis cases.

beats.narration_text: You don't have to believe any of these philosophers. The moves are tools, like a load test on a beam. The test finds a flaw, or it comes back clean. Either way, you've learned something.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one confident AI answer you rely on, and paste this into Claude: Here is an AI answer I rely on: paste it. Run three moves on it. One: what would have to be true for it to be wrong? List conditions I can check. Two: what may have changed since the evidence behind it was gathered? Three: rewrite it as a falsifiable claim that names the result that would prove it false. Then check two things yourself. Could you actually test each condition? And does the rewrite name a result that would prove it false?
